newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian hostage takers free more Shell staff.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian hostage takers free more Shell staff.

text.p: Nigerian villagers holding 88 staff of oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell as hostages have freed 35 and agreed to release the rest on Thursday, a company spokesman said.

"Another 35 Shell staff and contractors were released last night and brought safely back," said the spokesman in Lagos, adding: "Yesterday we met community leaders and an agreement was reached to release all the others today."

The hostage crisis began last Saturday when Ijaw tribesmen protesting the relocation of their local government headquarters to another town occupied six flow stations of Shell on which they detained 127 staff and contractors, all of them Nigerians.
Negotiations secured the release of the hostages starting with 18 on Monday and by Wednesday there were 88 still held.

The Shell spokesman in Lagos said the negotiations to secure the release of all the hostages had gone smoothly. "Everything is calm. The rest of the staff and contractors should be freed later today," he said.
Three Ijaw tribesmen have died in the protests which escalated into riots in the midwestern oil town of Warri on Tuesday while several houses have also been torched.
In Warri, Shell officials said those freed were from the Jones Creek flow station.

"The rest are in Egwa area and a boat is about to leave for them," said a Shell official, adding "The boat will be taking along some of the community leaders so that the people will not renege on their pledge."
"All injured people have been freed. Two who were seriously injured are at the sickbay in Shell in Warri," he said.

Ijaws three million people straddle the oil-producing swamps of Nigeria and are unhappy that the military government moved the headquarters of the newly created Warri South-West local government area to the rival Ogidigben town from Ogbe-Ijoh.
Similar relocations in other parts of Nigeria have also caused protests.
The current crisis does not directly involve Shell but the multinational is caught up in it because of its high profile in Nigeria and huge operations in the Warri area.

The attack on its installations caused Shell to shut down operations in the six stations, initially cutting back crude production by 100,000 barrels per day (bpd), about five percent of Nigeria's total output of almost two million bpd.

State-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation sources in London said on Thursday Shell's output had been cut by 210,000 bpd and the company may declare force majeure on some of the oil cargoes it was due to ship from April 2.
"Shell has advised us that there is every possibility" that they would declare force majeure from April 2, the source said.
World oil prices have been unaffected by the Nigerian situation.
Nigeria is Africa's largest producer of crude oil, and Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) with an output of about 2.15 million bpd.

Shell, which pumps about half the country's oil output, has often been the target of environmental protests and sabotage such as the those that forced its withdrawal from the volatile Ogoniland in 1993.
Shell's Nigerian operations came into worldwide focus in 1995 after Nigeria executed nine Ogoni tribe minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa.
Saro-Wiwa was leader of the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples (MOSOP), which had been campaigning against the company's environmental policies there.
